sceneFacts.proactivePrompt: What's the story behind Elle's iconic pink style?
sceneFacts.factHeader: Elle's pink wardrobe was a deliberate design choice.

factBeats.text: Elle's choice to wear a beaded bikini with pants and a hot pink fur coat while relaxing on campus was part of her iconic, predominantly pink wardrobe.
Costume designer Sophie de Rakoff decided Elle's signature color "has to be pink" after visiting sorority houses in Los Angeles.
De Rakoff elaborated that the specific shade was "a strong California pink that can survive in California light."
Reese Witherspoon had a clause in her contract allowing her to keep all of the outfits she wore in the movie.

sceneFacts.proactivePrompt: Discover the surprising origin of Elle's bunny costume.
sceneFacts.factHeader: Elle's iconic bunny costume had a surprising origin.

factBeats.text: The bunny costume scene is considered one of the film's "most iconic" moments.
Costume designer Sophie de Rakoff was responsible for creating the legendary look.
The famous ensemble "first came to life" in the stockroom of an intimates shop called Trashy Lingerie.
Sophie de Rakoff conducted the fitting for the costume in the back room of Trashy Lingerie.
Screenwriter Karen McCullah said Elle's confidence meant she would "stay in her costume the whole time and not worry about it."

sceneFacts.factHeader: "Bend and Snap" was a drunken bar invention.

factBeats.text: Producer Marc Platt wanted a B-plot for Paulette, leading screenwriters Karen McCullah and Kirsten "Kiwi" Smith to brainstorm ideas.
Initially, the writers considered a crime plot where the nail salon would be robbed.
Kirsten Smith spontaneously invented the move on the spot, describing it as a "completely drunken moment in a bar."

sceneFacts.proactivePrompt: Uncover the surprising story behind this iconic song.
sceneFacts.factHeader: Hoku's 'Perfect Day' was an underestimated anthem

factBeats.text: The song "Perfect Day" was originally intended to be the lead single for Hoku's second album.
Its inclusion in the film happened because the movie's production company was under the same umbrella as Hoku's record company.
Hoku recalled the film being presented to her as "this little movie" that "probably nobody's going to see it."
Despite the low expectations, "Perfect Day" ultimately became the most defining song of Hoku's career.
